title: Protocol for synthesizing and implanting polydimethylsiloxane in mice for imaging and electrophysiology
author: Takahashi, Huis in ‘t Veld, et al.
materials: Dental cement. (24). Black ink.(B) Surgical Procedure:
The headbar is temporarily secured using glue. (
The PDMS is covered with the cap. (

steps.title: Weigh base polymer
steps.instruction: Add 40 g Sylgard 184 polymeric base (Dow Inc.) into a plastic Petri dish; a layer of plastic wrap on the scale can prevent spills.

steps.title: Add curing agent
steps.instruction: Add 4 g Sylgard 184 curing agent (Dow Inc.) to maintain a 10:1 base‑to‑curing‑agent ratio.

steps.title: Mix components
steps.instruction: Mix the base and curing agent vigorously with a sterile stick for 5–10 min until the mixture is homogeneous; air bubbles will form.

steps.title: Degas under vacuum
steps.instruction: Place the mixture in a vacuum chamber at 0.05 mbar (room temperature) for 5–10 min, then slowly open the valve to let air re‑enter; bubbles rise to the surface and disappear.

substeps.instruction: Avoid rapid valve opening, which can disrupt the mixture.

steps.title: Repeat degassing
steps.instruction: Repeat the vacuum step multiple times until roughly 95 % of the bubbles are removed.

steps.title: Adjust mixture thickness
steps.instruction: Transfer the mixture to another smooth, flat plastic Petri dish to obtain a final PDMS thickness of 300–400 µm; for example, 2.89 g in an 8.5 cm diameter dish yields a theoretical 500 µm thickness, but the cured film will be ~100 µm thinner due to edge accumulation.

steps.title: Final degassing
steps.instruction: Repeat the vacuum step until no visible bubbles remain; if bubbles persist, extend vacuum time beyond 10 min (30 min–1 h) and repeat as needed.

steps.title: Cure PDMS
steps.instruction: Leave the Petri dish on a flat, minimally sloped surface for ~2 days to solidify fully, or accelerate curing in an oven; after solidification, measure thickness and use regions that are 300–500 µm thick.

steps.title: Cut PDMS windows
steps.instruction: On the day of surgery, cut the solidified PDMS into the desired shape (circular, hemispherical, etc.) using a biopsy punch, surgical knife, or scissors; 40 g base + 4 g curing agent produce 11 dishes, each yielding ~50 windows.

steps.title: Induce and maintain anesthesia
steps.instruction: Anesthetize the mouse with isoflurane 3.0–4.0 % for induction and maintain at 1.5–2.0 % throughout the procedure.

steps.title: Prepare surgical site
steps.instruction: Trim fur at the surgical site with a hair clipper, disinfect sequentially with 70 % ethanol then povidone‑iodine, apply ophthalmic ointment to the eyes, and administer lidocaine to the shaved skin for local anesthesia.

steps.title: Administer analgesia and anti‑inflammation
steps.instruction: Inject carprofen 5–10 mg kg⁻¹ subcutaneously for analgesia and dexamethasone 8 mg kg⁻¹ intramuscularly into a hind‑limb muscle to reduce brain inflammation.

steps.title: Expose skull and secure skin
steps.instruction: Incise the skin with surgical scissors, then secure the skin laterally to the skull using Vetbond; a scalpel may be used to retract skin but should not cut muscle.

steps.title: Place PDMS and outline craniotomy
steps.instruction: Place the PDMS window on the skull, draw the intended drilling outline with a black marker, ensuring the PDMS is smaller than the planned craniotomy.

steps.title: Attach headbar
steps.instruction: Attach a headbar to the skull with super glue; position it slightly left if covering the left hemisphere, gluing only the upper‑right side, leaving the lower‑left side elevated, and keep the bar parallel to the head orientation.

steps.title: Apply dental cement to headbar
steps.instruction: Cover the headbar with dental cement to begin stabilization.

steps.title: Provide intra‑operative hydration
steps.instruction: Approximately one hour into the surgery, inject saline subcutaneously to prevent hypovolemia and repeat the injection every hour for the remainder of the procedure.

steps.title: Drill skull
steps.instruction: Using a drill, thin the skull along the drawn outline until it moves when touched; start with a 0.9 mm drill bit to outline, then switch to a 0.5 mm bit to refine and thin remaining bone, smoothing the outer edge to avoid fragments.

steps.title: Prepare metal plate for compression
steps.instruction: Verify that the metal plate intended to press the PDMS can be positioned and angled within the craniotomy.

steps.title: Apply cold saline
steps.instruction: Apply cold saline to the exposed area.

steps.title: Flip skull flap and clean
steps.instruction: Using tweezers, carefully flip the drilled skull piece to expose the brain; wipe the craniotomy edge with a triangular sponge. Have cold saline, cotton swabs, and absorbable gelatin hemostatic sponges ready for potential bleeding.

steps.title: Control bleeding
steps.instruction: If bleeding occurs, apply cold saline again and wait until it stops before proceeding.

steps.title: Place PDMS onto brain
steps.instruction: Place a clean PDMS window onto the exposed brain; if the window is dirty, wash it with isopropyl alcohol and dry before placement.

steps.title: Press PDMS to skull level
steps.instruction: Press the PDMS window until it is level with the skull surface or slightly below; continuously monitor respiration and avoid excessive pressure that could depress breathing.

steps.title: Seal gap with thick glue
steps.instruction: Fill the gap between the PDMS window and the skull with thick glue, ensuring the glue does not adhere to the metal compression plate.

steps.title: Remove compression plate
steps.instruction: Slowly lift and remove the metal plate that was holding the PDMS in place.

steps.title: Seal with dental cement
steps.instruction: Apply dental cement over the thick glue, around the PDMS edge, and over the headbar; optionally mix black ink into the cement for stray‑light protection during calcium imaging.

steps.title: Add protective ring and cover
steps.instruction: Place a metal ring (1.8 cm diameter, 0.3 mm thickness, ~600 mg) on top of the headbar and secure it with dental cement; once the cement hardens, place a black cover over the ring. If a ring and cover are unavailable, cover the PDMS with dry gauze and secure with a metal plate, ensuring the PDMS is dry.

steps.title: Pull glass capillary
steps.instruction: Use a puller to fabricate a thin tip (~100 µm diameter) on a glass capillary for injection.

steps.title: Load capillary with solution
steps.instruction: Fill the pulled capillary with the viral or chemical solution (e.g., AAV mixed with Alexa Fluor 488) and attach it to a microinjector.

steps.title: Make incision in PDMS
steps.instruction: Create a small superficial incision on the PDMS surface at the region of interest using a 30 G needle; the incision need not reach the bottom of the window.

steps.title: Insert capillary
steps.instruction: Insert the pulled glass capillary into the incision.

steps.title: Approach dura mater
steps.instruction: Lower the capillary until it contacts the dura mater (defined as 0 mm on the dorsal‑ventral axis); if transparency is insufficient, add demineralized water—not tap water—to improve visualization.

steps.title: Penetrate dura
steps.instruction: Continue lowering until the dura is punctured; observe the rebound of dura and brain.

steps.title: Set injection depth
steps.instruction: Position the capillary at the desired depth for injection.

steps.title: Inject viral suspension
steps.instruction: Inject the viral suspension into the ROI, wait ~10 min, and repeat at additional sites if required.

steps.title: Withdraw capillary slowly
steps.instruction: Remove the capillary slowly to minimize backflow of the injected material.

steps.title: Protect window post‑injection
steps.instruction: Cover the PDMS window with a plastic cap or with dried gauze and a metal plate.

description: Recent advancements in neural activity recording techniques, such as calcium imaging and electrophysiology, as well as in neural control methods like optogenetics, have significantly improved our ability to examine the interactions of neuronal dynamics across multiple brain regions during perceptual tasks.1,2,3,4 These multimodal neuronal imaging approaches are particularly relevant in studies aimed at identifying and manipulating specific neuronal populations involved in sensory-motor and cognitive transformations, a process that involves interactions between multiple areas across the whole cortex such as conscious visual processing.5,6,7 To perform neural imaging across the whole cortex, the skull needs to be made transparent. Glass windows have long been used to enable functional, neuron-level imaging,8 but their rigidity makes them unsuitable for replacing the whole dorsal skull in long-term use over several months. Skull-clearing techniques9 do not suffer from this limitation, but, similarly to glass windows, do not allow mechanical access to the brain (e.g., for viral injections) without opening a craniotomy, a procedure which reduces transparency and increases the risk of infections. Finally, 3D-printed skull replacements have emerged to enable multi-site silicon probe recordings,1,10 but are not currently suitable for large-scale imaging. Flexible polymeric windows,11,12,13 e.g. made of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), potentially allow to overcome the limitations of the previously mentioned approaches, but standardized protocols to employ them are currently not available. To address this, we provide comprehensive, step-by-step instructions for synthesizing biologically compatible PDMS for use in neuronal imaging. We detail the surgical procedure for PDMS implantation, followed by methods for viral or chemical injections through the PDMS window.
